newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FEATURE - KPN aims for Dutch Internet revolution.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - KPN aims for Dutch Internet revolution.

text.p: The Dutch, proud of one of the highest PC ownership rates in Europe, justly have a reputation for adaptability to new technology.

But, although the ranks of Internet users in the Netherlands have swollen to around 700,000 from some 100,000 at the start of 1995, Dutch Internet usage is only of middling size in Europe, and research shows it is slowing.
Now the national PTT is gearing up to reach beyond the screens of its existing Net users and wire up around a quarter of its eight million telephone users by the end of 1998.

To do that Koninklijke PTT Nederland (KPN) is giving away a free e-mail address to each of its customers for an initial six month period in the hope of exciting their interest and turning them into full-blooded Net users.
"We want to get everybody hooked in getting on line," said KPN's Internet services director Herman Wessels.

"It's a chicken and egg situation, at least in Holland, and we want to make a breakthrough. If there's no mass market then the attractive applications won't come up. If there are no nice applications on the Internet then the mass market won't develop," he said.
KPN says it is planning to spend 600 million guilders ($317.2 million) over 2-1/2 years to boost Internet business, investing in more Internet technology, dial-in structure and software.

Wessels said the move was one of the most aggressive in Internet thinking, aimed at familiarising newcomers with the technology and language of the Internet so that they could get down to the fundamental point of the Net. Business.

"Getting information from the World Wide Web is interesting but that's not what Internet is in the end. It's the transaction side, buying and selling...that's why we think the Net will be a success because it makes that more and more possible," says Wessels.
WHAT THE SCHEME INVOLVES

Subscribers would be offered a CD-ROM or disk set to lead them through a basic Net training package and provide software for services, including browsers, which would get them to the electronic sites of leading Dutch companies.
"In lowering the thresholds for the mass market it really has to become plug and play, you have to overcome your fear of knobs and things," Wessels said.

Subscribers would use the software to create a very limited Internet look-alike which would give them access to Dutch firms keen to showcase their own goods and services and not have them tucked away in a vast maze of Internet information.
To get out onto the World Wide Web network and be truly hooked up to the Net subscribers are going to have to sign up with an Internet Service Provider (ISP).
Wessels denied KPN was out to poach ISP business, saying: "We don't want to step on the toes of ISPs, we don't want to give their business away, we want to support their business."
BUSINESS STRATEGY

Behind the strategy is hard-headed business. KPN hopes to exploit two earnings streams, one from increased phone line usage, and the other from companies wanting to reach out to phone subscribers directly.

With Internet calls charged at the local rate Wessels sees no disincentive to potential Net surfers. Neither does he see the straight telephone network groaning under the strain of extra calls as new infrastructure is introduced.

"The traffic generated by Internet usage has quite a different character from PSTN (public switched telephone network) traffic. We're dividing the Internet Protocol traffic at an early stage in the infrastructure," said Wessels.
"It's so cheap. It's less than two guilders an hour, it's the local telephone call rate. A lot of people using small amounts (of capacity) in the end is still a lot of money," he said.

Companies, too, are lining up to get in on the KPN act. They want clear Internet profiles and are prepared to pay for them. And if everyone picks up an e-mail address then there is an easy, big target for marketing drives.
"From a direct marketing point of view that's a very interesting feature and marketers are going to pay us for the mega-bytes of traffic involved," said Wessels.
OTHER SPIN-OFFS
Another spin-off attracting commercial interest is that companies can use the extra dial-in facilities created in the e-mail project for telecommuting by their own workers.
"We didn't think about that side two months ago, we were not aware that there was also an important market for teleworking using the same technology," said Wessels.

"Our first incentive was getting things up and running and starting the engine in using Internet technology more and more. The same infrastructure can be used for teleworking as well and that's a very important issue for the larger companies."
Another benefit for subscribers could be using the Internet for phone calls. Calls from a Net terminal can go anywhere in the world for the price of a local call.
The drawbacks are the cost of investing in the hardware and the fact that quality is lower than voice telephone lines because of the nature of Internet infrastructure.

"In fact there's so much infrastructure in between...that it's not a guaranteed quality. For business purposes today it's not good enough. If you have two people talking to each other, not using their mother tongue, speech quality has to be perfect for business," said Wessels.

"But if your family lives abroad, say in Australia or Canada, it's wonderful to talk for more than an hour for less than two guilders, it doesn't matter if you have to repeat things every now and then."
He says there's no reason for KPN to shy away from Internet telephony as the world is changing and companies are better off facing and embracing change.

"I don't think for the near future it's damaging normal telephony. Why shouldn't we support it? It's a fact of life, you can't take the new world away and block your company from new developments. We want to generate more traffic. A lot of newcomers are going to use it and generate traffic," he said. ($ = 1.891 Dutch Guilders)
